title: Earning to give
content:
By [Benjamin Todd](https://80000hours.org/author/benjamin-todd/) · Last updated November 24, 2026 · First published September 2014 ·

> _I was earning more money than I ever had, I was earning more money than my parents. It was like “Wow — I just graduated from college, and I’m able to earn a lot of money.” So to give 50% seemed like the least I could be doing._
> 
> 
> Jeff Kaufman on WBUR

Earning to give is the idea that instead of working directly to tackle a pressing problem, you take a job where you earn more money than you would have otherwise and donate much of the extra to fund others doing effective work on that problem.

The basic case in its favour is that if you’re a better fit for a higher-earning job than one directly working on, say, [preventing catastrophic pandemics](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/preventing-catastrophic-pandemics/) or fighting global poverty, you might be able to make a bigger contribution to these same causes via donating.

This isn’t usually seen as a virtuous career path. But we think there’s a lot to be said for it, and despite some serious potential downsides (which we’ll discuss how to mitigate), we believe it should be on the shortlist for some of our readers to consider.

For an idea of how it works in practice, consider the case of Jeff Kaufman who, along with his wife Julia Wise, is a parent of three children in Boston.

![Image 1: Jeff and Julia have tried to find the best way to make a difference](https://80000hours.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/Jeff-and-Julia-make-a-difference.png)

[Quartz:](http://qz.com/515655/this-couple-lives-on-6-of-their-income-so-they-can-give-100000-a-year-to-charity/) Jeff and Julia have tried to find the best way to make a difference

Through his relationship with Julia, Jeff became interested in using his career for good. He got a job as a software engineer at Google, earning a very generous salary that enabled the couple to give an unusual amount to charities they believe do exceptional work, particularly those recommended by the organisation [GiveWell](https://www.givewell.org/).[1](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-1)

They have [publicly pledged](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/pledge/?utm_source=80k&utm_medium=website&utm_content=earning-to-give-jeff-julia) to give away 30% of their income every year, though they have typically aimed to give away as much as 50%. The couple publicly shares their annual income and the [donations](https://www.jefftk.com/donations) they’ve made, for transparency and as part of their advocacy for others to donate to effective charities.[2](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-2)

“Over the past 13 years, my wife and I have donated about $2 million to charity — about half of that to GiveWell’s recommendations,” Jeff told the radio station [WBUR](https://www.wbur.org/onpoint/2022/12/21/what-is-the-effective-altruism-movement) in December 2022. “GiveWell’s estimate of cost per life saved has varied over this time, but if you put it sort of conservatively at around $5,000 per life, then 1 million divided by 5,000 is something like 200 [lives saved].”

“I feel very proud of that.”

## What is earning to give?

We say someone is earning to give when they:

*   Work a job that they believe is morally neutral or positive, and that pays more than they would have earned otherwise
*   Donate a large fraction of the extra earnings, typically 20-50% of their total salary
*   Donate to organisations they think are highly effective (i.e. funding-constrained organisations working on big, neglected problems)

In practice, many people earn to give in standard professional jobs. Some found companies or work in higher-paid finance careers in order to donate even more, but these paths do not represent the typical case.

These ideas aren’t wholly original to us. John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, preached about a version of earning to give in the 18th century. He advocated [the principles](https://www.whatsaiththescripture.com/Text.Only/pdfs/The_Use_of_Money_Text.pdf): “Gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.” And he even caveated this advice with sensible constraints, saying in a sermon that we shouldn’t work so hard that we hurt ourselves and that we should “gain all we can without hurting our neighbour.”[3](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-3)

[](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/)And famously, [Friedrich Engels](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Friedrich-Engels/Partnership-with-Marx) worked in textile manufacturing management in order to have enough money to support Karl Marx as he was writing _Das Kapital_. Since Engels viewed Marx’s writing as particularly important and potentially highly impactful, this decision is closely aligned with the ideas behind earning to give.

## Why earn to give?

Earning to give has been the most memorable and controversial part of our advice, attracting media coverage in the [BBC](http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/education-15820786), [Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2013/05/31/join-wall-street-save-the-world/), [Daily Mail](http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-2334682/Young-professionals-joining-Wall-Street-save-world.html) and many other outlets.

For this reason, many people think it’s our top recommendation for the majority of people. But it’s not. **Whether you should choose earning to give depends on your situation.** For example:

*   Earning to give might be your most impactful option if you’re an excellent fit for a high-earning path and don’t have other equally great opportunities on the table.
*   Earning to give can also be your top option if you really want to work in (or are already working in) a higher-earning path and don’t want to switch, or if you haven’t been able to find a job working directly in a high-impact area that suits your needs.

There are a lot of advantages to earning to give.

### It gives you flexibility.

The first major advantage of earning to give is its flexibility. You can use donations to support _any_ cause.

We recommend focusing on [highly neglected global problems](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/), but because these areas are small, it can be hard to enter them. Many people don’t see an easy route to working on something like preventing catastrophic biorisks, nuclear war, or AI alignment.

By earning to give, however, it’s possible to convert your skills (whatever they are) into additional work on pressing problems.

Even better, you can switch where you donate over time. This is very valuable, because which problems seem most pressing will change, as more research is done and as the situation evolves. Other factors will also change, like which solutions are most effective and which organisations are doing the best work.

Many other career paths involve taking a bet on a specific approach, and it’s hard to know how promising that will seem ten or twenty years in the future. But donations can more easily be targeted towards the biggest areas of need at the time.

### You may be able to have a greater impact

Second, if you’re a good fit for a higher-earning path, it’s sometimes possible to have a bigger [scale of contribution](https://80000hours.org/articles/leverage/) through your donations than through your labour.

Jeff’s story is one way to illustrate this idea.

By working at Google, Jeff was able to earn enough to pay for the salary of several non-profit CEOs at the time.[4](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-4)

|  | Google software engineer | Nonprofit CEO |
| --- | --- |
| Salary | $250,000 | $65,000 |
| Donations | $125,000 | $0 |
| Money to live on | $125,000 | $65,000 |
| Direct impact of work | Neutral | Very positive |

We can’t simply conclude from this that Jeff was having more impact than he could have had by working in the non-profit sector. For one thing, there may not have been any good non-profit CEOs around who needed additional funding in Jeff’s areas of interest.

And in fact, in 2022, Jeff left Google and earning to give to do direct work at the [Nucleic Acid Observatory](https://www.naobservatory.org/), which is developing a wastewater monitoring system in the hope of catching future pandemics earlier. He and Julia still donate a significant fraction of their family’s income, but the total amount is much lower than when Jeff was earning to give, and they now expect most of their positive impact to come directly from their work.

But the table does illustrate that earning to give can enable you to contribute just as much – if not more – than other impact-focused careers, at least under certain circumstances. And for some people, earning to give might be an _extraordinary_ option; if you become very wealthy and commit your fortune to address pressing global problems, you might support the work of hundreds of people who are a better fit for working on those problems.

If done right, this kind of earning to give would be an enormous achievement. But _doing it right_ is a huge caveat here, and there are serious perils in this kind of ambition. We’ll discuss the potential downsides later on.

One way you can gauge the trade-off between earning to give and other work is to ask top organisations working on the problems you think are most pressing whether they’d value your future work or your donations more highly. For instance, if you think you could donate, say, $30k per year, you could ask whether they’d prefer that or for you to join their staff and not donate anything.

The worse your fit for the more directly impactful job and higher your earning potential, the higher the relative contribution you can make via earning to give, and vice versa.

It’s not always possible to ask the trade-off question between giving and directly working so explicitly in practice. And if you’re early in your career, it’s hard to assess your long-run potential in the direct path. But thinking about the question helps to structure how to think about the choice.

There’s an odd thing that happens in the non-profit sector where someone with a very high salary (e.g. a corporate lawyer who bills at $1,000/hour) volunteers many hours a week to help out a charity. This can be seen as especially generous.

But if that lawyer had instead worked an extra hour and donated their earnings, they could have funded 100 people to help the charity instead. If they enjoy their work as a lawyer, this choice might be much less of a personal sacrifice than doing difficult minimum-wage work, but giving the money is likely _far_ better for the charity and its beneficiaries.

### Earning to give may allow you to work in a field that’s more personally fulfilling compared to other paths.

A third advantage of earning to give is that you might have a strong personal preference for a career that isn’t directly relevant to one of the problems that seem biggest and most neglected to you. Jeff, for instance, just happened to really enjoy his software engineering work at Google. Having an impact is probably not your only goal in life, and earning to give can help to open up options that might better meet your personal preferences while still having a lot of impact.

For example, if you have to support dependents, it might not be feasible to take a low-wage non-profit sector job. By earning to give, you can have a higher income than you would have in the non-profit sector and still do a lot of good.

### What if you want to donate part of your income but don’t want to earn to give?

If you don’t want to change your career in order to donate more (or aren’t ready to), but you still want to use your income to help others, you can start by donating some of it to effective charities.

[Here’s](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/best-charities) some advice on where to donate.

You might even consider taking the [🔶10% Pledge](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/pledge) from Giving What We Can — where you pledge to donate 10% of your income over your working life to whichever charities you think are most effective. (To test it out, you can [pledge 1% of your income for a limited time](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/get-involved/trial-pledge).)

This can be a way to ramp up to earning to give, or just to have an impact without affecting your career choice. For example, many of the staff at 80,000 Hours have taken the 🔶10% pledge — we’ve found it to be a meaningful way to help others, even outside of our day-to-day work.

You can take the pledge in just a few minutes. It’s likely to be the most significant thing you can do **right now** to do more good with your career.

[Pledge now](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/pledge/)

## Common objections to and reasons against earning to give

### Might you do harm in a high-earning career?

Yes, some high-earning careers can do a lot of harm. We don’t recommend taking careers you think might be harmful in order to donate.

First, if the harm done by the work offsets the good done by your donations — including both direct and indirect harms — then that’s clearly overall negative for the world and bad by any lights.

But even if you think the donations might outweigh the costs of a harmful career, we think doing harm “for the greater good” is almost never a good idea. And if you think you might be the exception, you’re almost certainly not. This is for many reasons, so we’ve written a separate article about why [not to take a harmful career in order to do more good](https://80000hours.org/articles/harmful-career/).

An illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the stated goal of earning to give.[5](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-5) We previously featured him on this page.

After billions of dollars of [customer funds went missing](https://www.wsj.com/articles/ftx-says-8-9-billion-in-customer-funds-are-missing-c232f684), FTX collapsed into bankruptcy and Sam was [convicted of fraud](https://www.npr.org/2024/03/28/1241210300/sam-bankman-fried-ftx-sentencing-crimes-crypto-mogul-greed).

Sam’s actions caused a lot of harm to individual depositors and society, both through the money lost and the indirect harms of criminal activity. It may have also harmed the reputation of the causes he was supporting and the idea of earning to give in general.

It now seems clear that even if Sam told himself that the rewards justified the risks, that was totally wrong on any view.

For our part, we felt betrayed and shaken when we found out what had happened, and we regret our past promotion of him (see [our mistakes page](https://80000hours.org/about/credibility/evaluations/mistakes/#ftx-2022)).

We only recommend people earn to give in jobs that are socially positive or neutral. Within any high-earning career, it’s vital to avoid actions that seem clearly wrong from a commonsense perspective, even if they might help you donate more.

### Is there a risk of getting corrupted by a higher-earning career?

Yes, and this needs to be taken seriously.

One risk is that your altruistic goals fade over time, and you don’t end up donating.

This is especially likely if you work in an industry with other people who aren’t very focused on doing good. The people you spend most time with have a huge effect on what seems normal to you – if all your friends are talking about the latest Ferrari, it’s going to be hard to stick to your plans to donate.

Some ways to counteract this are to:

*   Make a public pledge of your intentions to donate, such as through the [🔸10% Pledge](https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/pledge/?utm_source=80k&utm_medium=website&utm_content=earning-to-give-power-corrupts), or the [Founder’s Pledge](https://founderspledge.com/) if you’re an entrepreneur
*   Make sure to [spend time with others](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/community/) who are earning to give, donating or focused on social impact
*   Find other ways to remind yourself of the impact you’re having, like meeting people at the charities you support

We were very worried about people who intend to earn to give simply not donating when we started 80,000 Hours, but over the last ten years, we have seen a lot of people stick to their plans by taking the measures above.

A more worrying risk is that power corrupts. This is a cliche for a good reason.

This is most worrying in paths where you might earn a very large amount of money, like Sam did.

In that case, even if you set out with the best of intentions, it could become very tempting to act unethically in order to protect your fortune.

Having a lot of money also gives you a lot of influence, which makes it very important that you make good decisions about how to use it.

These kinds of concerns are not a big deal for people in regular jobs earning to give — like accounting, private tutoring, engineering or medicine — but apply more to paths where there’s a small chance of making huge sums. They make us more concerned about _highly ambitious_ earning to give as a strategy, i.e. trying to become extremely rich.

Overall, we feel unsure how much to recommend a more ambitious form of earning to give, and it probably depends on the person.

One thing to note is that this problem is not only a problem unique to earning to give. Rather, it’s a feature of _all_ careers in which someone gains power, influence and status. This could include working in politics or government, running any kind of large organisation, or being a well-known figure in your field. And those positions _are_ often ones where you can do a lot of good.

There will always be a temptation to act unethically in order to protect your power and status, and this temptation might grow the more of it you have. Likewise, it will also become more and more important that you’re able to act wisely with the power you’ve accumulated.

But taking the position that all altruistically minded people should avoid paths where they might accumulate significant influence doesn’t obviously seem better for the world.

And the stakes are high: in the case of earning to give in particular, you may be able to donate hundreds of times more in some paths than others.

What seems clear is that if you’re [aiming high](https://80000hours.org/articles/be-more-ambitious/), it’s important to set up safeguards. In addition to the points bulleted above, it’s very important to surround yourself with advisors who you trust and who are strong-willed enough to call you out if you start to drift.

If you start a company, it’s also important to set up more formal corporate governance structures, as an additional check on unethical behaviour and poor decision making.

And it could be worth making rough plans in advance for how you will distribute the money in a responsible way in advance, ideally delegating or decentralising the decision making in some way.

### Doesn’t taking a high-earning job signal support for a bad system?

Maybe. In general, it’s important to consider both the direct effects of your actions, and the indirect effects they might have via changing social norms and influencing others.

If you think the current general economic system is very bad, and that taking the job in question could significantly influence others towards greater support of the system, then that would be a significant negative for this strategy.

You’d then need to judge whether that negative was big enough to offset the other advantages of this path. (As did [Engels](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#engels)).

Also consider that there are ways that earning to give sends a positive signal. After all, giving away 20% or even 50% of your income, and giving it to neglected issues like helping the global poor or preventing another pandemic, is a very rare thing to do, and so it signals significant dissatisfaction with the results of the current system. And it shows that you’re willing to actually put your money where your mouth is in addressing problems that you see — potentially encouraging others to join you.

If you’re unsure about where you stand on this issue, you should probably spend more time evaluating other options that feel less like they contribute to a system you view as overall harmful.

### Isn’t charity ineffective?

Many charities probably aren’t that [effective](https://www.givewell.org/giving101/The-Wrong-Donation-Can-Accomplish-Nothing), so it’s vital to think hard about where you donate the money.

However, for earning to give to be impactful, you only need to find one effective charity to donate to. We think there are plenty.

One example [we’ve written about is the Against Malaria Foundation](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/making-a-difference/). A typical college graduate donating 10% of their income there could save about 40 lives over the course of their career. If you’re able to donate a bigger percentage or earn more than average, then you could do even more.

For more ideas, see the section below on how to give effectively.

Also note that if you think more mainstream charity is ineffective, you could use the money to fund academic research, political campaigns or to invest in socially impactful businesses instead.

### What if I won’t find earning to give motivating?

That’s fine. Do something else. It’s really important to find a job you’re good at and that fits with [the rest of your life](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/job-satisfaction/).

### What if I think X is higher-impact?

Great! Do that instead! We think there are lots of other impactful options, some of which we [list here](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/). And there are probably many others we’ve missed.

## Should _you_ earn to give?

We don’t think earning to give is typically the best way to make an impact, but we think it is worth many people at least _considering_ as an option among others.

We also often think of earning to give as a measurable baseline for how much good you could do: think about the highest-earning career you’d be able to pursue and thrive in that you think is morally neutral or positive; estimate how much you could donate; and then estimate how much good that could do if donated to the best charities you know about.

That’s probably already a lot of impact, which is hopefully motivating.

And then if you’re willing to make bigger changes to your life, you may well be able to find something even more impactful again. You can use the quantity of donations you can make in earning to give as a baseline to compare those other options.

We think earning to give is most worth considering when:

*   **You’re a good fit for a higher-earning option.**
*   **You want to gain [skills and career capital](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/career-capital/) in a higher-earning option** to use in other impactful paths later and earning to give could help you to stay engaged with social impact while you do so.
*   **You’re very uncertain about [which problems are most pressing](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/most-pressing-problems/).** Earning to give provides the most flexibility because you can easily change where you donate, or even save the money and give later. (Though many other paths are also highly flexible. If you become a great manager at a nonprofit focusing on biorisk, you can probably transfer that to organisation-building in climate change.)
*   **You want to contribute to an area that is more funding-constrained** rather than [talent constrained](https://80000hours.org/2015/11/why-you-should-focus-more-on-talent-gaps-not-funding-gaps/).

Overall, earning to give typically ends up seeming most attractive in the following cases:

*   You might be able to take a path that’s morally neutral (or positive) and where you might be able to donate _a lot_ (e.g. in certain parts of tech entrepreneurship, finance, partner-track in professional services etc.), and aren’t aware of other highly impactful paths. In this case, it might be your highest-impact option.
*   There’s a particular job you really want to do for other reasons that’s higher-earning than average, or that can be adapted into. This might look like Jeff working as a software engineer, or someone who really always wanted to be a doctor, or a teacher who does private tutoring and donates the extra.
*   You’re already in a path with good earnings, it’s going well and you don’t want to change careers right now.
*   You’re not aware of other good ways to contribute to [pressing problems](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/) that seem like a good fit for you right now, or are something you want to do.

However, we think earning to give is still well worth considering as a way that many people could make a bigger contribution to pressing problems sometimes without making dramatic changes to their lives.

## What’s the best way to earn to give?

If you’ve already decided to earn to give, which particular career paths or jobs should you pursue it in?

Look for an option where you have great [personal fit](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/personal-fit/) — the chance to excel — that satisfies the following:

1.   Is higher-earning and has a good outlook
2.   Offers [flexible career capital](https://80000hours.org/career-guide/career-capital/), so you can switch out later if you change your mind
3.   Doesn’t [cause harm](https://80000hours.org/articles/harmful-career/)

### Which jobs are highest-paying?

In short, it’s jobs in finance, management, medicine, law, real estate and technology. You can see a lot more data in this [separate analysis](https://80000hours.org/articles/highest-paying-jobs/).

### What are some of the best options overall?

The following offer a good combination of pay, flexibility and outlook. We’ve also already advised people who’ve taken them and been satisfied.

Two particularly high-earning paths are becoming a [tech startup founder](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/tech-entrepreneurship/) and  
[doing quantitative trading](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/trading-in-quantitative-hedge-funds/); they allow you to build up widely valuable skills while potentially earning millions, but they are _very_ competitive. Some other promising options taken by plenty of people we’ve advised include:

*   [Software engineering](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/software-engineering/)
*   [Startup early employee](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/startup-early-employee/)
*   [Data science](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/data-science/)
*   [Management consulting](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/management-consulting/)
*   [Marketing](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/work-in-marketing/)
*   [Medicine](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/medical-careers/)

In all of these, you could earn far more than the average for a college graduate, while also putting your career in a better position for the future.

[Law](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/high-end-law/) and [investment banking](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/front-office-finance/) are other obvious high-earning options, but we think they’re a bit worse than the ones above based on their weaker combination of flexibility, growth of the area, and direct impact. [Art and Entertainment](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/pursuing-fame-in-art-and-entertainment/) can be highly paid, but the chances of success are so small that the pay is low on average.

The following are somewhat less competitive ways to earn a medium income, though at the expense of less flexibility:

*   [Actuarial science](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/actuarial-science/)
*   [Executive search](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/executive-search/)
*   [Nursing](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/nursing/)
*   [Allied health](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/allied-health-professional/)

If you don’t have a college degree, real estate, programming or sales can be good options. Some trades are also highly paid. For instance, the top 10% of plumbers earn over $99,000 per year,[6](https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/#fn-6) more than what the average college graduate earns.

There are many paths we haven’t reviewed. Someone can earn to give in any career.

As a final note, some companies match charitable donations 1:1, or even more. By [choosing an employer that does this](https://80000hours.org/2013/05/how-to-double-your-donations-with-no-extra-effort/), you may be able to double your donations with no effort.

### Which charities are most effective to donate to?

Once you’ve earned some spare money to donate, where’s the best place to give it?

title: Different rules for the boss
content:
Of course, bosses have always been in favor of this. It’s one of the attractions of being the boss.

A consistent set of rules is easier to understand and enforce. One set of rules for behavior, reward and consequence is easier to justify from a moral perspective as well.

And yet, as Sahlins and Graeber wrote about in [_On Kings_](https://geni.us/ClrU4ew), the subjects of kings often _approve_ of their royalty having different rules. The king comes from away, he (and it’s often a he) has a different origin and a different destiny. Different rules for a different sort of person. Superman comes from Krypton, not from Smallville.

Someone who can act without facing consequences is a demonstration that he isn’t an ordinary person, and that is the closest thing on earth to a god. For some, “He doesn’t play fair” isn’t a flaw to be overlooked. It’s a credential.

The challenge for kings is that once the subjects decide that there is no magic, the past transgressions aren’t considered a sign of power, they’re the end of the line. Monarchy is brittle. Fun while it lasts, perhaps, but it often ends poorly.

# The Small But Mighty Brains of Bumblebees

Sometimes the best thinkers come in tiny packages

[DR](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

By [Devin Reese](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

11:00 AM CST on November 25, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/AdobeStock_380920104.jpeg?w=2880)

Bright macro shoot of the bumblebee sitting on the colourful flower. High quality photo

As humans, we credit our large brains, which contain [upward of 86 million neurons](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11884752/), for our intelligence. But our superiority complex has been gradually dampened as other tiny-brained species, [such as bumblebees](https://nautil.us/bumblebees-have-chimp-like-problem-solving-abilities-despite-tiny-brains-1281708), prove able to rival us on at least some cognitive tasks. In a [recent commentary](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aek1724) published in _Science_, biologists reviewed the brain capabilities of bumblebees (genus _Bombus_), asking, “What are the minimal neural requirements for intelligence itself?”

The study authors, biologists Lars Chittka at Queen Mary University of London and Stanley Heinze at Lund University in Sweden, reviewed the cognitive feats that bees have been able to accomplish—for example, [rolling a ball to climb up and reach nectar](https://nautil.us/bumblebees-have-chimp-like-problem-solving-abilities-despite-tiny-brains-1281708) in an enclosure too cramped for flying and learning to move latches to open puzzle boxes.

**Read more: “[Bumblebees Bounce to the Beat](https://nautil.us/bumblebees-bounce-to-the-beat-1279553)”**

At the same time, bumblebee brains contain fewer than a million nerve cells, a pittance of circuitry compared to our great network. So, their intelligence—defined in this study as “the ability to adapt to new situations by using cognition rather than instinct or trial and error”—stems from something else. The researchers explored aspects of bee brain architecture that might explain not only their problem-solving skills but also their “emotional contagion,” whereby bees transmit optimism about an anticipated food reward to nestmates.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Bumblebee brains contain a “mushroom body,” a region where associative memories are made in special neurons called Kenyon cells. It’s found in some other invertebrates as well, but bees have the monopoly with about 50 times more than, for instance, a fruit fly, a difference that could explain bees’ superior memory capacity. The study authors noted that the mushroom body architecture looks like the hippocampus in mammals, the area responsible for memories and recall. Maybe, they hypothesized, the “increased complexity of the mushroom body in bumblebees could have led to the evolution of additional, hippocampus-like circuits that conduct advanced com­putations such as pattern completion.”

Compared to fruit fly brains, bumblebees also have extra neural wiring associated with navigation, explaining how their brains calculate the optimal routes between multiple food sources—like a built-in GPS system. Plus, bumblebees have a more elaborate neuromodulatory system, which likely allows them to more subtly distinguish “between similar but not identical situations that might otherwise evoke the same action.”

It remains to be determined whether these special brain features evolved as neural wiring customizations on a simpler insect brain or just gradual boosts in computational abilities.

Regardless, it’s hard not to consider bumblebees as big-brained—no matter how tiny their physical brains might be. ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This Clever Marketing Tactic Works on Rats Too
content:
In 1918, the SS _Makambo_, a steamship, ran aground on Lord Howe Island off the coast of Australia. The ship was only out of commission for nine days and lost just one passenger, but what seemed to be a relatively minor maritime snafu soon spiraled into a full-blown ecological disaster.

Black rats stowing away on the ship disembarked and made the island their home. Over the years, their populations exploded, wreaking havoc on the island’s native flora and fauna and threatening the livelihood of the people living there. To combat the rodent invaders, Australia undertook a lengthy and costly eradication program. Over a century later, in 2023, they were finally able to declare victory.

**Read more: “[How Invasive Rats Mess with Coral Reef Food Webs](https://nautil.us/how-invasive-rats-mess-with-coral-reef-food-webs-1283294)”**

According to a new paper published in the _Journal of Applied Ecology_, they might have been able to save some time and money if they used a little bit of nudge marketing.

Imagine you own a restaurant with a few bottles of wine on the menu priced at $20, $40, and $60. The most expensive wine on your menu also comes with the highest markup giving you the most profits, but it’s not selling. You could lower the price to $50 to make it a more attractive purchase eating into your margins, but a wiser strategy might be adding a fourth bottle priced at $100. While the extravagantly priced wine may be out of reach for most customers, it makes the $60 bottle look more attractive in comparison, psychologically nudging them to buy it.

But does it work on rats?

To find out, a team of environmental scientists from the University of Sydney set up hundreds of trap-like tunnels around their city wired with cameras. Inside the tunnels they placed plain white bread (which rats will definitely eat, even if it’s not their preferred food) or tastier jam sandwiches. Outside they placed phantom decoys—metal shakers filled with peanut butter balls (which rats love) that they could smell, but couldn’t reach.

[Video 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/Videos-with-and-without-decoy.mov)

A video comparing rat entry into a trap with a phantom decoy outside with entry into a trap with standard bait. _Credit: Peter Banks and Jenny Bytheway_

Remarkably, these peanut butter-scented phantom decoys increased rat entries into the boring bread-baited tunnels by a whopping 83 percent. (However, they didn’t have an effect on the traps baited with jam sandwiches because entries were already high.) To determine whether rats were just attracted to the smell of peanut butter, the team placed the shakers at the back of the tunnels, but entries remained low. In other words, the phantom decoys seemed to be psychologically nudging the rats to make (what turned out to be) an unwise “purchasing decision.”

“Improving rodent trappability has been a millennium-long challenge for humanity that’s never been tackled from a nudge theory approach before,” study author Jenna Bytheway said in a [statement](https://www.sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2026/11/24/marketing-tactic-used-to-trap-invasive-rat-species.html). “This approach is a simple, low-cost way to improve pest control and wildlife monitoring by changing how animals perceive their choices when lures alone aren’t enough.”

It can save quite a bit of money, too. The last rodent holdouts on Lord Howe Island proved to be incredibly elusive and therefore expensive to snag. “The initial eradication of 300,000 rats and mice on Lord Howe Island cost $57 per individual, whereas capturing the 96 rats discovered 2 years later cost $18,750 per rat,” the researchers wrote.

At the end of the day, marketing—even directed at rats—is all about the money.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Heat Made Life
content:
The idea that life is not _on_ Earth but _of_ Earth is an old idea that goes back at least a few hundred years. Charles Darwin, for instance, was interested in how certain forms of life, such as worms and corals, reshaped the Earth’s crust. Before Darwin, Jean-Baptiste Lamarck also noticed that certain geological features of the planet, like limestone cliffs and mountains, were made not just from the remnants of dead marine organisms, but by living ones.

Over the last couple of years, interest in this idea of the interplay between Earth and life has witnessed a revival, with the publication of Ferris Jabr’s _Becoming Earth_, which highlights how life shapes and is shaped by rock, water, and air; and Andrew Knoll’s _Earth and Life_, which emphasizes the geochemical cycles that connect biology and geology over the course of Earth’s 4-billion-year history**.**

Now, a new book tackles this relationship between Earth and life with originality and depth: _The Co-Creation_. Author Olivia Judson, who is both a veteran science writer and an evolutionary biologist, makes an argument that life has shaped and been shaped by Earth through a series of five major energy “expansions” in the history of the planet.

Judson’s argument offers a new framework that connects major events in the history of life on Earth: its very origin, the rise of photosynthesis, the dawn of the eukaryotes, the emergence of animals, and the central role fire played in the evolution of our species. The book also wrestles with the question of what life is, and how we might recognize it elsewhere in the universe.

I recently talked with Judson about why conceptualizing life in terms of energy rather than information is an ancient idea that got eclipsed during the era of molecular biology—and why it’s experiencing a resurgence now.

**Can you tell me about the genesis of this book?**

I came to the idea that the planet we experience today is to a very large extent the result of the past activities of life forms almost 20 years ago, when I was writing a regular column for _The_ _New York Times_. There were a couple of different things that really struck me.

One was this article by mineralogist Bob Hazen and some of his colleagues that made the argument that most of the mineral diversity here on Earth today is the result of the activities of life, either directly or indirectly. I was surprised because I hadn’t thought about the diversity of minerals being something that life could increase—and not just increase, but increase so massively.

I also came across a paper that was looking at the way that bacteria can modify the magnetic fields of rocks. At first, this sounds like magic. But it’s actually quite straightforward. What happens is the bacteria do various sorts of chemical activities that result in, for example, a mineral called magnetite—one of the magnetic minerals—being transformed into a different mineral, which doesn’t have magnetic properties. The result is that life forms can affect magnetism. For me, that was also revelatory.

I decided that I was going to look into it, and here I am, more than 15 years later, still looking into it.

**WONDER BOOK:** Writing about energy and life forms, Olivia Judson says, increased her sense of amazement and empathy. _CREDIT: Alexandre Courtiol_

**In the book, you argue that a defining feature of life is that living creatures are “servants of energy”—that they actively seek energy. Can you elaborate on this somewhat abstract idea? Why do you choose energy, and not information or DNA, as the central concept in defining life?**

Carl Woese, who was one of the people who discovered the archaea [a type of single-celled microbe], says in a 2004 paper that life forms are eddies in a flow of energy.

And when I first read that, it just didn’t make any sense to me because it’s so very different from the way that I had been brought up to think about life. I was educated at Stanford and at Oxford, and I say this not to be boastful, but more to indicate the kind of indoctrination that I received, where information was the whole thing. The emphasis, insofar as there was any emphasis on evolution at Stanford back then, was about genetics. And Oxford was the home of my PhD supervisor, W.D. Hamilton, but also Richard Dawkins, who wrote _The Selfish Gene_. So everything was about genetics.

If you look at writing from the 1910s and the 1920s, people are thinking a lot about energy and evolution, but that fades away as the nature of the gene is discovered. People then become obsessed with information. But actually, you need to think about both. Information on its own can’t do anything. Energy is what allows any activity.

Thinking about sand dunes was what helped me to understand this idea that life forms are a pattern in an energy flow. It helped me to understand because the dunes have so many lifelike activities. But the differences between life forms and sand dunes can also help us to understand what sets life forms apart from other structures. The essential argument is that life forms belong to a general category of structure, which I’m calling “energons,” where the form is sustained by the flow. Ilya Prigogine, who won the Nobel Prize and so has a better claim to be making neologisms than I do, called such things “dissipative structures.” But for me, the name energon feels more related to energy somehow.

What is unusual and sets life forms apart from other energons is the ability to consume internal energy in order to get more energy. But writing any kind of definition can be an extremely hair-tearing process. I think it’s very difficult to set a clear circle around any phenomenon.

**What are some of the implications of thinking about life in this way?**

The principal thing that I would like to point out is this idea that energy is first, and all activity is a consequence of energy. One way to demonstrate this to yourself very simply is to feed a cookie to a child. What happens is the child starts running around and screaming. This is a consequence of the input of energy. I think that seeing life forms as servants of energy has greatly changed the way that I see many activities of life forms, in particular human activities. I now think that a firework display is essentially a spectacle of energetic servitude. We’re drawn to it. We like it. Fast cars, another spectacle of energetic servitude.

That is a manifestation of something that might be very deep. And thinking in terms of energy helps to expand an understanding of ourselves. It helps to expand an understanding of the natural world.

**In the book, you talk about five energy expansions in the history of life: rock, light, oxygen, flesh, and fire. Let’s start with the first one, rock, which stands in for geochemical energy. What do we know about how life arose from rock?**

The first thing I should say is that the idea that there was a transition from geochemistry to biochemistry is the argument that makes the most sense to me. Now, exactly how life started is not established, and may never be established. Even if we were able to generate life forms from scratch in a laboratory, it doesn’t mean that’s how it happened here. The question is what happened, and that’s a question that dates back around four billion years. Nevertheless, the idea that a flow of energy and materials can form structures, and that the energy could come from chemical reactions between water, rocks, and gases, strikes me as fundamentally plausible.

The idea is that you have chemical reactions going on between water, rocks, and gases. These chemical reactions are similar to those that take place within life forms, and that adds an element of plausibility as well, because some hypotheses for the origin of life invoke chemistries that nothing uses. And it is more intellectually satisfying to me to think that there has been a continuum, that the processes of the Earth led to the processes of life in a way that we can still see and recognize today.

Supporting this philosophical outlook is the fact that there are life forms that make energy entirely from water, rocks, and gases. These life forms [microbes that live in hydrothermal vents] have no requirement for organic materials. The fact that such life forms exist means that they could have done well early in the history of the Earth.

This is actually one of the places where [evolutionary biologist] Bill Martin’s work has been especially influential on my thoughts. It’s through thinking about Bill Martin’s work that I understood the extent to which the evolution of biochemistry is something that could potentially be investigated and traced.

It’s very, very difficult because four billion years separates today’s life forms from the earliest life forms. But nevertheless, intellectually or philosophically, one can start to think about the likely pathways that biochemistry may have developed along. Thinking about biochemistry as subject to evolution has helped it to become more accessible to me.

Credit: Envato / GreensandBlues

**The final expansion is fire. Does this expansion, and maybe those before, offer new ways to think about the environmental crises of climate change and biodiversity loss, or does it primarily serve as a lens for understanding the past?**

Fire is a phenomenon that has its own fossil record. It appears to have come into existence with the evolution of plants on land, which is relatively late in Earth history, around 430 million years ago, possibly a little earlier. But fire as a source of energy for life is something that I think is a trait of humans.

I subscribe to [anthropologist] Richard Wrangham’s view and the view of his colleagues that fire is one of the things that made humans what we are today. That the evolution of cooking provided a way for us to expand the range of food that we could eat and also to get more calories from the same food than we could before. So it expanded our own personal access to energy and reshaped the human form, in particular resulting in smaller jaws, smaller teeth, smaller stomachs, and larger brains. There are also obviously a lot of other advantages to cooking, including killing off a lot of bugs, so it’s also outsourcing the immune system to some extent. It also reduces the costs of digestion, because you’re basically doing a pre-digestion. So in terms of human evolution, I think it’s been hugely important.

In terms of human cultural evolution, it’s been hugely important as well, especially in the ways that it has allowed us to expand our own metabolism. In particular, the use of fire made new technologies possible and also enabled access to new kinds of energy to support these technologies. And for me, this view of fire has fundamentally changed how I see humans. I think it really places us as part of a continuum of the life/Earth story.

Today, a lot of people say they’re very disconnected from nature, but actually collectively we’re more connected than anything has ever been before. Because we’re having more impacts, and we’re having them faster. Yes, cyanobacteria [which produce oxygen] transformed the atmosphere in collaboration with the Earth itself, but they took many, many, many millions of years to have this transformative effect. We’re having these effects over the last 200 years. It has helped me to understand what is happening, and perhaps it also helps us to think about what we could do.

**There’s a lot of excitement right now about astrobiology, and the idea that understanding the fundamental features of life on Earth might lead to the discovery of life forms elsewhere. What’s your view of the search for life in the universe?**

The discovery of life elsewhere would be tremendously exciting, obviously. At the same time, we don’t have to go to Mars to know that whatever has happened there is fundamentally different from what has happened here. It would obviously be fascinating to know, but if there is something there, it’s _very_ difficult to find. In contrast, this planet, Earth, just screams “alive!”

This planet is, in my view, the most interesting planet that any of us will ever know anything about. Far and away. This is not to say that I’m uninterested by other places and what might be going on. But I think we’re here in this unique place, and we know about it and we can study it, and it is extraordinary. This work has increased my sense of wonder, it has increased my sense of amazement, it has increased my sense of empathy. It has made me just so fascinated by all life forms. I think that we have such a rich place, and it is so layered. There are so many different layers and all of these different kinds of energy being captured and channeled. It’s just a marvel. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# When Stars Collide: Astronomers Have Spotted a First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger

A quick, violent, super-bright end as two stars become one

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

7:00 AM CST on November 25, 2026

Our telescopes and their data-scanning algorithms are getting more and more powerful over time. As such, previously never-before-seen celestial sights are now regularly coming into view. The latest example: a pair of stars merging, where one of the pair is at a particularly late stage of life, and surrounded with a diffuse, extended cloud of gas, something that’s called common envelope evolution (CEE).

In this particular case, a super-giant star, around seven times the mass of our sun, swallowed up a smaller star with around a tenth of the mass, creating an incredibly bright eruption. A team of astronomers, via the James Webb Space Telescope, was able to analyze the system’s behavior before, during, and after the merger, which is unprecedented. Until now, the existence of CEEs has mostly been a theoretical idea.

![Image 6](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/bao_inline2.jpg?w=710)

An artist’s concept of four of the merger’s key stages. _Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI/Leah Hustak (STScI)/Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia)_

It all happened in the Andromeda galaxy, a nearby neighbor of the Milky Way, some 2.5 million light-years away. The newly single star has been nicknamed Bao, and it may have been rejuvenated by the extra-stellar material (it’s still too early to tell).

**Read more: “**[**These Stars Swallowed Their Earth-like Planets**](https://nautil.us/these-stars-swallowed-their-earth-like-planets-1281535)**”**

The whole process—from the smaller star getting snagged on the outer edges of the larger one to being completely engulfed—took just seven years, a relatively speedy resolution for something that can take centuries. A full record of the merger has been [published](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z) in _Nature_, marking the culmination of observations that began back in 2023. “We thought it would take centuries for an outburst to happen, and then one day it erupted,” study author Nadia Blagorodnova said in a [statement](https://www.astro.columbia.edu/news/columbia-researchers-spot-first-its-kind-stellar-merger). “We were flabbergasted.”

The common envelope evolution is so-called because the two stars involved share parts of their gas cloud with the other. This time around, when the smaller star’s envelope came into contact with its much larger neighbor, it lost its orbital energy and was pulled in.

But CEE scenarios don’t always end in mergers. It’s thought that both stars can sometimes transform into other states, including black holes and supernovae explosions.

Thanks, though, to some diligent stargazing and sky-mapping, we know exactly how this one played out. And as study author Kishalay De [put it](https://www.astro.columbia.edu/news/columbia-researchers-spot-first-its-kind-stellar-merger), “These surveys are opening up completely new avenues to study dying stars and perhaps even discover new phenomena we haven’t seen before.” ![Image 7](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace

No ice deliveries needed

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

3:00 PM CST on November 24, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/01-fire.jpg?w=2880)

It’s one of the most fundamental questions about life on Earth: How did water get here?

[Video 5](https://nautil.us/earths-water-may-have-formed-in-this-fiery-furnace-1287019)

[Video 6](https://nautil.us/earths-water-may-have-formed-in-this-fiery-furnace-1287019)

One possibility is that it was delivered as frozen ice by a bombardment of meteorites smashing into our planet’s surface. Another is that the chemistry of the early Earth somehow produced water from molten rock—a theory that’s the focus of a new study [published](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02138-3) in _Nature Geoscience_.

**Read more: “**[**This Paradoxical Desert Landscape Is Filled with Fresh Water**](https://nautil.us/this-paradoxical-desert-landscape-is-filled-with-fresh-water-1283495)**”**

The researchers behind the hypothesis are calling it “pebble rain” (or “pebble accretion”). What happens is silicate rocks with iron inside, drawn toward Earth by its increasing mass and gravitational pull, react with hydrogen in the atmosphere. Given the high speeds, high pressure, and high volume of incoming rocks involved, the subsequent chemical reactions could have stripped away the oxygen from the iron in the pebble showers, releasing water vapor as a by-product.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

The researchers estimate that around 200 oceans’ worth of H2O may have been released in this way, supplying the planet with the magic ingredient for life. These pebbles would have been external visitors, like meteorites, but the water would’ve been formed on Earth rather than in space.

What’s more, the same process could plausibly happen on other planets as they form too—opening up new possibilities in our search for extraterrestrial life. “Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites,” study author Zachary Sharp explained in a [statement](https://news.unm.edu/news/unm-research-suggests-earth-may-have-formed-much-of-its-water-as-the-planet-grew). “Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism.”

The researchers simulated the conditions of the early Earth in their lab with temperatures of up to 2,552°F, and heating silicate rocks in streams of hydrogen. Almost 80 percent of the iron oxide in the samples turned into metallic iron, producing water vapor along the way.

“Looking out over a large body of water, it’s hard to imagine that that water may have been produced four-and-a-half billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere,” Sharp said, “but it very well may have.” ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Even Tiny Bits of Exercise May Help Regulate Blood Sugar

When you can’t have an exercise meal, have an exercise snack

[JC](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

2:00 PM CST on November 24, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/shutterstock_2753752001.jpg?w=2880)

In the Soviet Union, workplace exercise breaks were mandatory. At set times during the day, everyone from the factory floor to the accounting department would pause their jobs for a brief bout of calisthenics. While pushing back from your desk to do jumping jacks might earn you some odd looks from coworkers, “exercise snacking” (as it’s apparently being rebranded) can also take the form of brisk five-minute walks. According to a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/oby.70349) in the journal _Obesity_, these snacks might also help some people control their blood sugar levels.

“We often say exercise snacks are a stepping stone for someone who doesn’t do any exercise or cannot do a single bout of exercise,” study author Ana Pinto of the University of Colorado School of Medicine explained in a statement. “Any movement counts.”

**Read more: “[Gentle Exercise May be More Effective Than Medications at Managing Chronic Pain](https://nautil.us/gentle-exercise-may-be-more-effective-than-medications-at-managing-chronic-pain-1285269)”**

Pinto and a team of exercise scientists and fellow metabolic researchers recruited 30 sedentary adults who were either overweight or obese and split them into two groups. The first group went on 45-minute walks at a brisk pace five days per week. The second group went on five-minute walks 10 times a day on the hour. During the six-week study period, the participants wore a glucose monitor, and they received an intravenous glucose tolerance test before and after.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

The team found that the group with hourly bite-sized walks maintained tighter control over their glucose than the once-a-day walkers. Exercise snackers’ time within normal glucose range rose from 82 percent to 94 percent, while it fell from 89 percent to 80 percent for the other group. They also had improved glucose tolerance, or the body’s ability to maintain normal blood sugar levels after a meal.

Curiously, the steadier glucose profiles of the exercise snackers came from fewer dips instead of blunter spikes. The team speculated the liver, prompted by more frequent activity, could be releasing glycogen to keep things running smoothly. Neither group showed any changes in insulin sensitivity.

Of course, there were some caveats. There was no control group in the study, the sample size was relatively small (and consisted of only overweight or obese people leading sedentary lives). Most importantly, diet was outside the scope of the investigation.

Still, if you’re feeling guilty about not exercising at all, a five-minute walk every hour can’t hurt. “The message is, reintroduce movement in your daily life,” study author Audrey Bergouignan of the University of Colorado School of Medicine said. “As humans, our biology was naturally selected at a time when we were physically active. So as a culture, as a society, we need to think about and reimplement putting movement back into our daily lives.” ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# No Pumbaa Needed: Meerkats Are Great Solo Navigators

But they’re still best off sticking with their gangs

[DR](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

By [Devin Reese](https://nautil.us/author/devinreese)

1:00 PM CST on November 24, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/AdobeStock_250084692.jpeg?w=2880)

Meerkats are highly social animals, living in related gangs of up to 50 individuals to guard their colonies and care for their pups. They even forage together, setting off every morning as a group to search for insects and other small creatures. Because they’re always together, it’s difficult to tell which meerkats have the spatial knowledge to lead the group out and back home again. That said, you’d expect experience to play a role in their navigation abilities, such that some individual meerkats would get lost without their group.

To test this theory, for a [recent study published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1242/jeb.252200) in the _Journal of Experimental Biology_, researchers from Switzerland, alongside volunteers at the Kalahari Research Centre in South Africa,experimented with tracking individual meerkats (_Suricata suricatta_). They captured 20 teenagers or adults from five wild groups in the Kuruman River Reserve and fitted each with a GPS radio collar that in some cases also recorded sound.

**Read more: “**[**It Takes a Village to Raise a Meerkat**](https://nautil.us/it-takes-a-village-to-raise-a-meerkat-237456)**”**

Each radio-collared meerkat was returned to its colony, then scooped up the next morning and released 1.5 kilometers away, alone but still within its colony’s broader territory. Researchers trailed and filmed the behavior of each meerkat as it tried to find its way home. Most of them followed a fairly straight path, stopping every now and again to look or sniff for landmarks. All but two made it home—and those two males were, of course, eventually returned to their colonies. Even the younger, less experienced meerkats were adept navigators.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

“This suggests that daily life in a meerkat social group provides ample opportunities for spatial learning, enabling all group members to navigate independently,” [concluded the study authors](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151708).

It’s worth noting, however, that once meerkats found their way back to their original capture points or sleeping burrows, a handful of them failed to unite their groups within the three hours of the study period. It turns out, finding their neighborhoods was easy, but figuring out where their friends were was much more of a challenge. ![Image 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
